I'll use this opportunity while it's still early to share my experience with Argon.

I got it via the "Pro" plan, exclusively for personal task usage. So no agentic programming.

For starters, the limits are dreadfully low. Five messages on medium is already enough to trigger a 4 hour cooldown. Secondly, the best part is the integration with Google search and Maps. Makes it seamless for trip planning. Lastly it's the only "SOTA" model in a long time that has actively hallucinated details. I don't know if it's because the Gemini harness is not asking it to verify information, but I've had some real Deepseek V3-like lies in responses.

Either way, I find it difficult to get invested in Gemini because nobody will have access to Carbon for a few months anyways.

Doesn't mean jack without access to it.

But with this bs of not making it even public, pushing off release of newer models late, I lost faith in Google.

Especially with the recent addition of graphic visualization widgets

It manages to strike the perfect balance between depth and style of prose that other Frontier models just can't quite seem to match

Gemini team has a long history of releasing great benchmark charts and disappearing into the ether. There has never been a moment where I have preferred them to Claude/Codex. When I get access I eval them on my home assistant set, a small coder benchmark, etc. and they are too expensive, and too low quality.

The benefit for Google is their chat interface has privileged access to their data (maps, etc.) but their model itself is low quality and, if I'm being honest, has the promotion-oriented measurable-output bias that FAANGs tend to have. The later Llamas had the same problem.
Carbon scoring below Opus 5.5 on coding highlights how magnificent Opus 5.5 is as a coding agent. With just a $20/month sub, it performs a ton of work at a very high quality.

As of their latest update (AA's), I find their index hard to trust, and a bit shady. 60% of the benchmarks contributing to the AA index are now private, nobody can replicate them. And they explicitly say that they offer benchmark consulting to labs. This is a serious conflict of interest.

The latest update knocked down only openweights models from the leaderboard.

I tried Argon for a large historical HTR transcription project recently, since I heard it was really good at this. It was really good, but like all top US models I've used it was

* Definitively very good at domain specific knowledge. It can read sloppy 19th century danish gothic handwriting with faded ink just fine. Not perfectly, but probably better than I could have done with a day of struggle for every page.

* Expensive.

* Bad at actually doing what I said. I had told it in the prompt to be careful not to miss text, but I hadn't explicitly told it that some images may have text in double-column layout. So on those images - over half of my 300-page document - it produced an excellent transcription of the first column, and then considered itself done. Want to try again with a more careful prompt? That'll be another $20.

You know what. When Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview came out it was better than Opus at the time. It was my main model for 3 weeks.

Until it got lobotomised. Then it lost most of it's capability.

Similar situation happened to Anthropic's Fable. It was an amazing model until Opus 5.5 came out.

So now, I'm not even looking at a "new" model until it is a month or two old. By then we will know if they will destroy ability to make it cheaper to host.

The benchmarks of a model that hasn't been released yet are definitely suspicious.

I also think Google should stop "releasing" models that aren't actually available. For their own sake, because by the time Gemini 4 Carbon becomes available, nobody will notice. There won't be a new press release or much excitement around it.

I want to talk about my experience with Argon, noting that I used it via OpenRouter on a Raspberry Pi, spending around $15 in credit.

My experience is that Google is aiming to create a generalist model – but a truly generalist one! In fact, I find it particularly accurate in general terms and even in long conversations, maintaining excellent consistency and a wealth of information in response to complex questions.

I’ve tested it both as a coding agent – though, precisely because of what I mentioned above about its ‘generalism’, I don’t think it measures up to Fable 5.1 or Astra – and I’ve really appreciated its qualities when supervising my agents’ activities. It was able to keep track of them, suggest alternatives, and monitor the entire lengthy process in parallel without ever straying too far from the request or losing the thread – as often happens with Claude and OpenAI (you only need to test it in Claude Code itself, in both Ultracode and the agent team mode – albeit experimental – to realise how, once the task gets underway, both of them lose their way).

Just so everyone is aware of the "coincidences" that happen with this index:

- Two days ago AA announced their v5 Index which added a few new benchmarks and tweaked a few things.

- Today the newest model announced from a big lab tops the charts.

I'm not saying that AA is definitely taking money from the big labs and changing the benchmark to make the labs' new models look better, but it kind of looks that way. This pattern of behavior has happened before, where the index gets tweaked right around when a new model comes out, and the new model is on top. AA does not, AFAIK, provide a way to see how the new models would have scored under the older index versions. You could probably calculate it yourself, but I'm not going to do that much legwork just for an HN comment.

It's interesting because they publish the index methodology, so you can't really accuse them of not being transparent, but I don't really believe that the choices to update the index were completely independent of the model they happened to be evaluating at the time.

Related: The DXOMark camera scoring method also had similar behavior, where they would release new testing methodology right before flagship smartphones were released. Again, they are technically being transparent about the process, but it kind of smells like the "independent" testers may not be as independent as the average user would hope.

Artificial Analysis is not trustworthy anymore. Every time an open-weight model, especially Chinese, looks to be nearing the top, AA updates the index to (ostensibly) specifically push closed models higher. Just recently with v5, OpenAI models were pushed up.

These benchmarks and rankings seem more noise than signal these days. They're uniformly divorced from sincerely-attested real world experience. And the real world experience isn't driving any consensus either.

So here's a meta-benchmark: at what point does the act of choosing an LLM product for a reasoning task become less reliable (in the sense of "predictive of future success") than hiring a human being for that same task? Have we already cross that threshold? I think we might have.

And once we do... what happens then? Will the truly elite models be hidden in a sea of mediocrities simply because the goofball "managers" doing the hiring are too dumb to recognize their genius?

The time between public announcement -> public release seems to be a tacit admission that Google is still a bit behind the frontier labs. Google is justifying the delay by pointing to cyber risk and a closed-access period reserved for analysis of safeguards. I'm dubious of this justification. But if it is true, I'm pretty sure the other labs are doing similar sorts of things in private. I think most of us prefer it that way—if Anthropic public announced Fable 5.5 two weeks ago with no availability that would add to my annoyance. Maybe they learned their lesson with Mythos, or  maybe it's just that Google also does not have an IPO looming. Who knows?
